title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.709-6 (06/2015): Parameter values for the HDTV standards for production and international programme exchange
key_findings: In-force HDTV standard: 16:9, 1920x1080 active, square pixels; Y'CbCr with chroma sampled at half luma frequency

Primaries R(0.640,0.330) G(0.300,0.600) B(0.150,0.060), white D65 (0.3127,0.3290); OETF V=1.099L^0.45-0.099 (L>=0.018), V=4.5L below (values read in the BT.1886 appendix table, which reproduces BT.709)
BT.709 defines the camera-side OETF but NOT the display EOTF (that is BT.1886)
practical_applications: Tag every SDR delivery bt709 primaries/transfer/matrix
sRGB and BT.709 share primaries, so Chrome-rendered HTML frames and video can match if tagged and range-converted correctly
limitations: Full PDF text not parsed this session; primaries/OETF read via BT.1886 appendix

title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1886 (03/2011): Reference electro-optical transfer function for flat panel displays used in HDTV studio production
key_findings: Reference EOTF L = a(max[(V+b),0])^gamma with gamma = 2.40, a and b derived from screen white LW and black LB
10-bit code D maps V=(D-64)/876; reference black D=64, white D=940 (8-bit equivalents 16/235)
Measurement of conformance recommended in a dark room; BT.709 never documented an EOTF because CRTs behaved alike
practical_applications: Grade SDR for gamma 2.4 dim-room reference; phones in bright rooms look lighter/flatter than the grading monitor — check on a phone
Limited (tv) range 16-235 vs full range 0-255 mismatches cause lifted blacks or crushed shadows
limitations: Copy hosted on a university teaching site; same text as ITU

title: A Standard Default Color Space for the Internet - sRGB, Version 1.10
authors: Stokes, M.; Anderson, M.; Chandrasekar, S.; Motta, R.
key_findings: sRGB uses BT.709 primaries and D65 white
Transfer closely fits gamma 2.2 with a small linear segment
Reference display 80 cd/m2; encoding viewing environment 64 lux, typical 200 lux
practical_applications: HTML/Chrome renders in sRGB (~2.2); video players decode BT.709 for ~2.4 displays — the same pixels can look slightly different; test the final MP4 on a phone
limitations: Document marked obsolete; the formal standard is IEC 61966-2-1 (not read)

title: YouTube recommended upload encoding settings
key_findings: MP4, no edit lists, moov atom at front (faststart)
H.264 High Profile, progressive, 2 B-frames, closed GOP of half the frame rate, CABAC, VBR, 4:2:0
Upload at the recorded frame rate (24,25,30,48,50,60); SDR 1080p 8 Mbps (24-30 fps) / 12 Mbps (48-60 fps); 2160p 35-45 / 53-68 Mbps
Audio AAC-LC/Opus, 48 kHz, 384 kbps stereo
SDR colour: BT.709 primaries, transfer and matrix
practical_applications: Use as the baseline for every platform master; deliver higher than the platform re-encode
limitations: Platform page changes without notice; re-check before each campaign

title: Understand three-minute YouTube Shorts
key_findings: Square or vertical uploads up to 3 minutes (on/after 15 Oct 2024) are categorised as Shorts; 16:9 is long-form
Shorts over 1 minute with an active Content ID claim are blocked globally
practical_applications: Render vertical masters <=180 s for Shorts; deliver 16:9 if a clip must stay long-form
limitations: No resolution/bitrate given on this page

title: Reels resolution and size (Instagram Help Centre, Thai locale)
key_findings: Reels may be uploaded between 1.91:1 and 9:16
Minimum 30 fps and minimum 720 px resolution
Recommended cover 420x654 px (1:1.55); cover cannot be changed after upload
practical_applications: Never deliver Reels at 24 fps from Wan without conforming to 30 fps; 1080x1920 master exceeds the minimum
limitations: help.instagram.com URL returned an empty shell; read via facebook.com/help/instagram mirror

title: Meta Ads Guide: Instagram Reels video ads specifications
key_findings: 9:16, recommended 1440x2560, MP4/MOV, max 4 GB, 0 s to 15 min
Keep text/logos/key elements out of top 14%, bottom 35%, and 6% each side
Primary text 44 characters; captions optional but recommended
practical_applications: Safe box on 1080x1920 = x 65-1015, y 269-1248 for anything that must be read
limitations: Ads spec, not organic Reels; Meta UI changes often

title: TikTok Auction In-Feed Ads video specifications
key_findings: Last updated June 2026
Non-Spark: 9:16 >=540x960 (recommended), 16:9 >=960x540, 1:1 >=640x640; mp4/mov/mpeg/3gp/avi; up to 10 min; <=500 MB; bitrate >=516 kbps
Safe zone depends on dimension, caption length and add-ons; TikTok gives downloadable templates, not fixed numbers
practical_applications: Use TikTok's template overlay at QC; keep a 1080x1920 master
limitations: Organic TikTok upload specs not on an official page found this session

title: EBU Loudness (R 128) technology page
key_findings: Normalise to -23 LUFS +/-0.2 LU (+/-1 LU live), relative gate -10 LU
Streaming supplement R 128 s2 exists (targets not given on the page)
practical_applications: Broadcast deliverables only; social platforms normalise differently — loudness detail belongs to the audio-engineering module
limitations: Max true peak not stated on the page; streaming targets not read

title: About Apple ProRes
key_findings: 4444 family carries alpha (up to 16-bit); 422 HQ is 10-bit 4:2:2 'visually lossless'
practical_applications: Use ProRes 4444 for transparent overlays (glasses cutouts, title layers) between tools; never upload ProRes to social
limitations: Rates are targets (VBR)

title: Shutter Angles & Creative Control (RED 101)
key_findings: Shutter angle expresses exposure time relative to frame rate; ~180 deg = ~1/48 s at 24 fps, 'by far the most common setting for cinema'
Larger angles smear motion; smaller angles look stuttered/disjointed (like 1950s newsreels)
practical_applications: Exposure = (angle/360) x (1/fps); for synthetic motion blur in HTML/AI clips, blur length ~ half the per-frame displacement mimics 180 deg
limitations: Vendor tutorial; no perceptual data

title: Evidence that Viewers Prefer Higher Frame-Rate Film
authors: Wilcox, L. M.; Allison, R. S.; Helliker, J.; Dunk, B.; Anthony, R. C.
key_findings: Stereoscopic 3D clips shot/projected at 24, 48, 60 fps with shutter angles (reported 90/180-358 deg): clear preference for higher frame rates, mainly 24 vs 48/60
Shutter angle had little effect except on motion smoothness for one clip type
practical_applications: 24 fps is a convention, not a perceptual optimum; HFR reads 'smoother/more real' — choose by intended feel
limitations: S3D content, specific clips; abstract-level only; shutter range reported inconsistently across listings

title: Perceiving layout and knowing distances: The integration, relative potency, and contextual use of different information about depth
authors: Cutting, J. E.; Vishton, P. M.
key_findings: (per secondary sources) depth information is integrated from many sources whose relative potency varies with distance: personal, action and vista space
(per secondary sources) binocular disparity is strong near, weakens with distance; occlusion and aerial perspective work at all/large distances; metric cues lose utility around 100 m
practical_applications: In a flat 2D/AI frame (no disparity) depth must be carried by occlusion, relative size, height in field, aerial perspective, blur and motion parallax
limitations: Closed access; boundaries (~1.5-2 m, ~30 m) only from lecture summaries, not verified in the chapter

title: The neural basis of depth perception from motion parallax
authors: Kim, H. R.; Angelaki, D. E.; DeAngelis, G. C.
key_findings: During observer motion, objects at different depths move at different image speeds — quantitative depth from geometry similar to disparity
In primates disparity is generally more precise than motion parallax
Motion parallax alone is ambiguous in depth sign; smooth eye-movement signals (and large-field 'dynamic perspective' cues) disambiguate
Motion-parallax demonstration as an independent cue credited to Rogers & Graham (1979)
practical_applications: 2.5D clips: speed ratio between layers is what reads as depth; a large textured background helps the brain resolve near/far sign
limitations: Neural/primate focus; read first ~90% of text

title: Motion parallax as an independent cue for depth perception
key_findings: Random-dot displays with no other depth cues: relative motion coupled to observer head movement produced vivid depth (corrugated surfaces)
practical_applications: Parallax works even on featureless texture — camera move + layered speeds is enough for depth
limitations: Not read; content from Kim et al. 2016 and search snippets

title: Blur and disparity are complementary cues to depth
authors: Held, R. T.; Cooper, E. A.; Banks, M. S.
key_findings: Disparity is more precise near fixation, blur more precise away from fixation; observers rely on the more precise cue
Contested: Vishwanath argued it measured blur discrimination, not perceived depth from blur; later work found blur can impair depth discrimination in naturalistic images
practical_applications: Shallow depth of field supports depth ordering away from the focal plane but is not a full substitute for layering/occlusion
limitations: PMC page blocked by bot check; findings from abstract-level snippets

title: Retinal blur and the perception of egocentric distance
key_findings: Blur gradients act as a quantitative distance cue: surfaces with blur gradients judged closer
Magnitude of blur strongly affects perceived scene scale — basis of tilt-shift miniaturisation
practical_applications: Strong blur top+bottom on a wide shot makes a real scene look like a miniature — avoid unless that toy look is wanted; use for playful product worlds
limitations: Abstract-level only

title: Experience can change the 'light-from-above' prior
authors: Adams, W. J.; Graf, E. W.; Ernst, M. O.
key_findings: Shape-from-shading uses a prior that light comes from above; the prior is modified by active visual-haptic experience
Later work: prior may be context-specific and depends on body orientation
practical_applications: Under-lighting reads as unnatural partly because it violates the light-from-above assumption — a reasoned (not proven) basis for 'horror' under-light
limitations: Full text not read; emotional reading of under-light is craft, not shown here

title: How the 'Rule of Thirds' is Wrong: Let us Count the ways (Palmer Lab, UC Berkeley, spatial composition research summary)
authors: Palmer, S. E. and lab (summarising Palmer, Gardner & Wickens 2008, Spatial Vision 21:421-449; Gardner & Palmer; Palmer, Hara & Griscom; Linsen et al.; Langlois et al.)
key_findings: Center bias: centre was the most preferred position for every object in every facing direction
Inward bias: right-facing objects preferred left of centre and vice versa — subjects should face into the frame; weakens with fast implied motion
Rule of thirds tested: 'results strongly contradicted both of the ROT's main claims'

Ecological position (eagles higher, stingrays lower) and ecological size (mouse smaller, elephant larger) preferences; 'representational fit': non-standard compositions preferred when context justifies them
practical_applications: Lead/look room has empirical support (inward bias); thirds is a heuristic only; centred framing is a valid default for a single hero product
limitations: Lab summary page; static images, not moving shots

title: Evaluating the rule of thirds in photographs and paintings
authors: Amirshahi, S. A.; Hayn-Leichsenring, G. U.; Denzler, J.; Redies, C.
key_findings: Computed rule-of-thirds scores vs ratings of 30 participants; later cited as finding no preference for ROT-conforming images
practical_applications: Do not score frames by thirds compliance
limitations: PDF not parseable; findings via search summary and Abeln et al. 2016 citation; exact title unverified

title: Quicker, faster, darker: Changes in Hollywood film over 75 years
authors: Cutting, J. E.; Brunick, K. L.; DeLong, J. E.; Iricinschi, C.; Candan, A.
key_findings: 160 films 1935-2010: shorter shots (~10 s -> <4 s), more motion, shorter shots carry more motion in recent films, and films got darker
Luminance = median 8-bit value per frame averaged per film; B&W vs colour nearly equal (132 vs 130); animation stayed brighter
Proposed reasons: greater dynamic range, less lighting needed, darker images in dark rooms give more attentional control
practical_applications: Dark low-key looks are a modern feature-film norm made for dark theatres — phone viewing in daylight argues for lifting mids for Reels
limitations: Hollywood English-language sample; correlational

title: The evolution of pace in popular movies
key_findings: 180 films 1930-2015: luminance falls through complication/development, darkest near the 3/4 point, rises through climax/epilogue — strong only in 1990-2015 films
Mean shot length 1990-2015 ~4.3 s
practical_applications: Empirical support for a brightness arc in a colour/lighting script: darkest beat ~75% through a story clip
limitations: Read ~55% of the article; descriptive data, not causal

title: Modest virtuosity: A plea to filmmakers old and young
key_findings: Ensemble staging in depth guides attention with performance, framing and lighting, reducing cuts
Techniques: actors advance/recede, blocking and revealing ('opening a slot'), still ancillary figures, head-blocking, off-screen space, delayed cutting
Main example: Panic in the Streets (1950, Kazan) two-minute scene in two shots; three depth zones in the mortuary scene
'cinematic space is calculated for one sightline, that of the camera'
practical_applications: Puppet/rig scenes: stage reactions in depth inside one shot instead of cutting to every line
limitations: Expert film-historian blog (B), analysis not experiment

title: Gradation of emphasis, starring Glenn Ford
key_findings: Charles Barr (1963): wide framing allows 'gradation of emphasis' — details at varying prominence
Priming: plant a secondary element early, pay it off later (Framed 1947 robe; 3:10 to Yuma 1957 out-of-focus figure behind Ben Wade; Best Years of Our Lives 1946 phone booth in depth)
'if you stress a secondary element too much, it becomes primary'
practical_applications: Plant the product/prop in the background of an earlier shot before it becomes the hero
limitations: Critical analysis

title: Figures Traced in Light: On Cinematic Staging
key_findings: Depth staging and deep-focus cinematography are distinct techniques (Renoir 1930s: much depth staging, little deep focus)
practical_applications: Depth staging does not require everything sharp; layered blocking works with shallow focus too
limitations: Book not read; from author's book page and blog

title: Filmmaking Theory for Vertical Video Production
key_findings: Vertical frame suits full-length people, tall/long-thin subjects, hand-to-face objects, corridors, stairs, Y- and Z-axis movement; X-axis action should be turned diagonal
A horizontal close-up framed in 9:16 fills ~4/5 of the screen — reads as big/extreme close-up; frame vertical 'close-up' down to the navel
Thirds struggles for looking room in vertical; proposes a 'rule of fifths'; wide lenses help show person + environment; long lenses thin the background
Power/vulnerability via top/bottom placement; entrapment feeling in narrow frame
practical_applications: 9:16 shot-size table and blocking rules in FD06
limitations: Author's reflective synthesis, not empirical; conference paper

title: The Visual Story: Creating the Visual Structure of Film, TV, and Digital Media (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Seven basic visual components: space, line, shape, tone, colour, movement, rhythm
Principle of contrast and affinity: more contrast in a component = more visual intensity; more affinity = less
Visual structure can be graphed against story intensity (taught in UT Austin RTF 318 'Graphing Visual Structure')
practical_applications: Plan flat vs deep space, tone and colour contrast to rise with the story climax
limitations: Book not read; from publisher/O'Reilly listings, reviews and a course wiki

title: Cinematography: Theory and Practice for Cinematographers and Directors (4th ed.)
key_findings: Chapters on lighting sources, lighting, image control, DIT and workflow; companion lighting demos at routledge.com/cw/brown
practical_applications: Standard reference for lighting and image-control vocabulary
limitations: Content not read; publisher page only

title: Color Correction Handbook: Professional Techniques for Video and Cinema (2nd ed.)
key_findings: Chapter 8 'Memory Colors: Skin Tone, Skies, and Foliage' covers memory colours, audience preferences and secondary corrections for skin
practical_applications: Order: primary correction -> secondaries (skin/sky/foliage) -> look
limitations: Only publisher listing and ToC read

title: ACES Documentation — Overview
authors: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (ACES Central)
key_findings: ACES2065-1 = linear AP0 interchange/archive; ACEScg = linear AP1 for CG; ACEScct = log AP1 for grading

Input Transforms bring camera data into ACES; Output Transforms (rendering + display encoding) prepare for a display; Look Transforms (LMT) apply creative/technical looks in scene-referred space; Reference Gamut Compression since ACES 1.3
practical_applications: Only relevant when mixing camera log footage + CG; our HTML/AI pipeline is display-referred sRGB/BT.709
limitations: ACES 2 pages listed but not read

title: Effects of color on emotions
key_findings: Saturation and brightness had strong, consistent effects: Pleasure = .69B + .22S; Arousal = -.31B + .60S; Dominance = -.76B + .32S
Brightness effects similar for chromatic and achromatic colours
practical_applications: In grading, brightness and saturation move feeling more reliably than hue: brighter = more pleasant/calm, more saturated = more arousing
limitations: Munsell chips, not moving images; abstract only

title: Color and emotion: effects of hue, saturation, and brightness
key_findings: Factorial hue x saturation x brightness design: emotional effects depend on all three and their interactions, not hue alone
practical_applications: Do not assign fixed emotions to hues; test the specific look
limitations: Abstract-level; patches not film

title: Shot Craft: Light Quality 101
key_findings: Quality = breadth of the light-to-shadow transition; set by source size relative to distance
Hard: small source far away; soft: large source close; diffusion/bounce becomes the new source; diffusion on the lens does little
practical_applications: Prompt soft light as 'large soft source close to the face', not just 'soft light'
limitations: Tutorial; negative fill not covered

title: Lives Under Siege: The Goldfinch and 1917
key_findings: Goldfinch: restaurant lit by practical candles with only background practicals; museum aftermath: ceiling SkyPanels dimmed near camera, brighter in distance (backlit silhouettes)
1917: shot under cloud cover so the one-shot continuity matched ('it was crucial that the dailies be even'); burning-church night lit by flames + flares, 360 deg dimmer rig
practical_applications: Continuity: lock one sky/key condition per sequence; for AI clips pin one light description across all shots
limitations: Case study

title: L.A. Confidential: Exposing Hollywood's Sordid Past
key_findings: Spinotti: practicals 'were quite often our key lights'; wanted their halos and burn-outs
Quarter-to-half blue gel for night bedroom; orange+magenta on a Xenon for low early sun 'pink and orange at same time'
Super 35 spherical lenses for wider apertures
practical_applications: Practical-as-key recipe for night interiors (night optic shop)
limitations: Case study

title: Flashback: Gordon Willis, ASC Interview at AFI (Part I)
key_findings: Overhead diffusion used discriminately; Godfather Part II darker because character/environment called for it
'sometimes it's better not to see what is going on until a given point in the scene'; decide the look before choosing how to light; start from existing practicals
practical_applications: Eyes-in-shadow top light is a motivated choice for withheld/secretive characters, not a default
limitations: Interview

title: The Art of the Mired Measurement
key_findings: Mired = 1,000,000 / K; a gel's mired shift is constant, so its Kelvin change depends on the source
Lee Full CTO +159: 5600K -> ~3000K; on 7000K -> ~3300K; Rosco Full CTO +167, GAM +146; 1/4 CTO +63
practical_applications: Compute warm/cool offsets in mired; colortemperature filter values in kelvin follow the same reciprocal logic
limitations: Trade-press tutorial; CTB values not given

title: Lighting ratios explained
key_findings: Cites ASC formula (key + fill) : fill
Maps 1 stop ~2:1, 2 stops ~4:1, 3 stops ~8:1 measured side vs side; 1:1 flat, 2:1 moderate, 4:1 dramatic, 8:1 noir/horror
practical_applications: Library ratios are lit-side : shadow-side incident readings (see convention note in FD08)
limitations: The stop mapping and the (K+F):F formula give different numbers for the same setup — convention conflict noted

title: What is the 'Orange & Teal Look' and Why is it So Popular?
key_findings: Teal shadows / orange highlights; rationale: skin sits in orange so a teal background separates the subject; golden-hour imitation offered as a guess
practical_applications: Rationale only holds when skin/product is warm and background can be cool
limitations: Summarises a LUT-selling tutorial; no evidence; no films named

title: Let's Examine the Three Aspect Ratios of 'The Grand Budapest Hotel'
key_findings: 1932 scenes 1.37:1, modern 1.85:1, 1968 2.40:1 anamorphic (article also says 1.33/2.35 — inconsistent)
Anderson: 'the different aspect ratios tell viewers where they are in the timeline'
practical_applications: Aspect ratio as a time/world marker inside one piece
limitations: Internal inconsistency in ratio figures

title: Mommy (2014) 1:1 aspect ratio — Screen Daily / CBC / AFC Turpin interview (search results)
key_findings: Shot mostly 1:1; widens to 1.85 for liberation/elation moment(s) then returns to square (count reported as one or two)
Dolan: square removes distractions, captures the viewer's vision with the character's gaze
practical_applications: Frame-size change as an emotional event; square/vertical = intimacy and confinement
limitations: Pages not opened (AFC 403); search snippets only

title: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B model card
key_findings: TI2V-5B: text- and image-to-video at 720P (1280x704 / 704x1280) and 24 fps
Wan2.2 training data labelled for lighting, composition, contrast, colour tone (claim for the family)
Weights released 28 Jul 2025
practical_applications: Our local wan.py also encodes 24 fps; conform to 30 fps (or build the timeline at 24) before Reels delivery
limitations: Capability claims are the vendor's; our 6 GB card runs 480x848

title: Depth Anything V2
key_findings: Teacher trained on 595K synthetic images pseudo-labels 62M+ real images; students 25M-1.3B params; NeurIPS 2024
Claims >10x faster and more accurate than Stable-Diffusion-based depth models
practical_applications: tools/depth.py uses the small model for 2.5D layer splitting; output is relative depth, not metric
limitations: Abstract-level

title: Vectorscope skin-tone line (I-line ~123 deg) — Videomaker / Boris FX / Resolve tutorials (search results)
key_findings: Skin-tone indicator line corresponds to the NTSC 'I' line (~123 deg), between red and yellow; skin of all shades clusters on or slightly around it
It is a reference, not a target — stylised warm/cool lighting may legitimately move skin off it
practical_applications: ffmpeg vectorscope check after any look; skin far off the line toward green/magenta = fix
limitations: Search snippets; no official Blackmagic statement of the angle
